teaser: Fruit, a cup and a rose. In 1633, viewers may have read them like a prayer.
review_notes:
Religious reading (offering to the Virgin; citrons for Easter, orange blossom and water for purity, thornless rose for Mary) is a widely repeated scholarly interpretation, not documented; the lesson says so.
The 'lemons' are usually identified as citrons (cidras).
Technical study at the Norton Simon found a plate of sweets (described as candied sweet potato) painted out by the artist; check exact wording and position.
Only signed and dated still life by Zurbarán (1633).
Zurbarán called to Madrid in 1634 to work for Philip IV at the Buen Retiro.
Juan de Zurbarán, still-life painter, died in the Seville plague of 1649.
Norton Simon (fortune from Hunt Foods) bought the painting in 1972.
Size about 62 x 110 cm.

lesson.text: The first people to stand in front of this canvas, in Seville in 1633, probably did not think of lunch. They lived in a city full of convents, processions and sermons, where everyday things carried sacred meanings. Three groups of objects lined up on a table, lit against black: to them it may have looked like gifts laid on an altar.

Many historians read it that way today. Orange blossom and clear water stood for purity. A rose without thorns was a common image of the Virgin Mary. The yellow fruit was linked with Easter. Put together, the table becomes a quiet tribute to Mary, with no figure in sight.

Nothing proves it, though. No letter or contract explains the picture, and Zurbarán left no comment. In Spain a painting of food and vessels was called a bodegón, a word that first meant a cheap tavern. This one is as far from a tavern as a bodegón can get.
The fruits on the left are probably not lemons at all. Their size and thick, knobbly skin point to citrons, an older cousin of the lemon that was candied or used for its scent more than its juice.

Whatever it means, the arrangement is the first thing that strikes you. Still lifes of the period often pile up abundance: spilled grapes, a cut ham, a knife hanging off the table. Zurbarán sets out his objects as if he had measured the gaps.
Three groups, one shelf, one light. See how strict the order is.

lines.label: The table edge
lines.text: The front of the table runs straight across, parallel to the picture's own edge. You face the objects head on, the way you face a shelf or an altar.

lines.label: The pyramid
lines.text: The leaves above the basket are the summit, the two metal plates are the corners. The lower groups sit like attendants on either side of the tall central one.

lines.label: The light
lines.text: Light comes from the left and a little above. Every object is bright on its left side and sinks into shadow on its right, which is why each one looks so round.

lesson.text: Notice too what never happens: nothing overlaps from one group to the next. Each plate and the basket has its own patch of table and its own pool of darkness behind it. The three groups are neighbors that do not touch, which gives the picture its hush.

Zurbarán was 35 and the busiest painter in Seville, known for monks and saints lit like statues in dark rooms. Here he turns the same hard light on fruit. The following year the king's court called him to Madrid to help decorate a new royal palace.

X-rays show that the composition was once more crowded. Zurbarán had painted another plate, holding sweets, and then covered it with the dark background. The famous emptiness was a decision made at the easel.
Order can carry feeling. By spacing a few plain objects evenly and lighting them with care, Zurbarán makes a kitchen subject feel solemn.

This is the only still life he ever signed and dated, which suggests he was proud of it. The best way to see why is to wander across the table yourself, from the rough peel on the left to the name he left on the right.

spots.title: The top citron
spots.text: The fruit on top shows its puckered end, a crater of wrinkles around the tip. The skin is dry and pitted, painted with thick yellow that catches the light.

spots.title: The pewter plate
spots.text: The dull metal rim reflects a soft yellow glow from the fruit sitting on it. Pewter is a gray alloy of tin, cheaper than silver and common on Spanish tables.

spots.title: Orange blossom
spots.text: White flowers and buds still cling to the sprig. Blossom and ripe fruit together are true to life: orange trees can carry both at once. Brides wore these flowers as a sign of purity.

spots.title: The basket
spots.text: A braided rim, then tight rows of wicker, each strand given a highlight. You can almost count them. The weave fades into shadow on the right side.

spots.title: The rose
spots.text: A pale pink rose lies on the rim of the plate, with no stem or thorns to be seen. It is the only soft, perishable thing among hard fruit and metal.

spots.title: The cup
spots.text: A white ceramic cup with two small handles, filled almost to the brim. The dark oval of liquid is usually read as water.

spots.title: The signature
spots.text: Faint strokes on the front of the table: his name and the year 1633, written as if on the wood itself.

lesson.text: Still life ran in the family. Zurbarán's son Juan became a gifted painter of fruit and vessels, with a darker, richer touch than his father's. He died at 29 when plague struck Seville in 1649, an epidemic that killed about half the city.
The painting now belongs to a museum founded by Norton Simon, a California businessman who made his fortune in canned tomatoes and other packaged foods. He bought it in 1972.

So a food magnate ended up owning the most austere plate of fruit in Western art. Nobody in this picture will ever eat. The citrons stay whole, the cup stays full, and almost four hundred years later the rose has not dropped a petal.

quiz.question: How might a viewer in 1633 Seville have understood this table?
options: As an advertisement for a fruit seller
As an offering with religious meaning
As a scientific study of plants
quiz.explanation: Many historians think the objects were read as symbols honoring the Virgin Mary.

quiz.question: What did “bodegón” first mean in Spanish?
quiz.explanation: The word for a tavern came to name paintings of food and vessels.

quiz.question: What did X-rays reveal under the dark background?
options: A plate of sweets that Zurbarán painted out
quiz.explanation: He removed a plate, making the composition emptier on purpose.

quiz.question: What are the yellow fruits on the left most likely to be?
quiz.explanation: Their size and thick, knobbly skin suggest citrons, a cousin of the lemon.

quiz.question: From which side does the light fall?
quiz.explanation: Every object is bright on its left side and shadowed on its right.

facts.text: Zurbarán signed and dated many still lifes.
facts.explanation: This is the only one he signed and dated.

facts.text: The three groups of objects do not overlap one another.
facts.explanation: Each group has its own space on the table, which gives the picture its calm.

facts.text: A document from 1633 explains exactly what the objects symbolize.
facts.explanation: No such document exists, so the religious reading remains an interpretation.
